paper.title: Career Effects of Mental Health
paper.journal: NBER Working Paper Series, Working Paper 29031

registers.name_in_paper: Central Psychiatric Register (Landspatientregistret for Psykiatri Diagnoser)
registers.role: treatment: all mental health diagnoses from psychiatric departments in Denmark, classified by ICD-10
treatment measurement: all prescriptions from all doctors and hospitals in Denmark, used to measure lithium usage and to extend the BD indicator

registers.name_in_paper: registry data on earnings (wages and income from self-employment; Appendix Table A1)
registers.role: outcomes: earnings, zero earnings, position in the earnings distribution
outcome: indicator for receiving disability benefits

registers.name_in_paper: family identifiers (mother's or father's anonymized social security number)
registers.role: linkage: links each person to their siblings and parents; available for 1,788,166 people (71 percent of the population)

registers.name_in_paper: parental financial assets reported by banks and other financial institutions
registers.role: heterogeneity: socio-economic status measured by the parents' median percentile in the distribution of assets

registers.name_in_paper: unemployment data (indicator for being unemployed for one day or more within the year)
registers.role: controls and sample splits: unemployment spells around a diagnosis; log unemployment rate as a control

linkages: Individuals linked to their siblings using their mother's or father's anonymized social security number as a family identifier (available for 1,788,166 people, 71 percent of the population; 75 percent of all people have one or more siblings, 82 percent among people with BD)
Mental health diagnoses linked to earnings, disability and unemployment records at the individual level
Individuals linked to their parents' financial assets to compute the parental wealth percentile
Diagnoses combined with lithium prescriptions from the Prescription Register to identify people with BD

sample.universe: The population of Denmark in birth cohorts 1946 to 1977: 2,692,479 people, of whom 97,932 were diagnosed with depression, 22,694 with BD and 41,813 with schizophrenia between 1995 and 2015
selection_rules: Individuals born in cohorts 1946-1977 in the Danish population registers
Observed in person-years in which they are aged 20-60
Calendar years 1995-2015 (the years for which psychiatric diagnoses are available)
Log-earnings and earnings-distribution outcomes: restricted to person-years with positive earnings
Family-fixed-effect specifications: restricted to people with a family identifier (1,788,166 people, 71 percent of the population)
Parental-wealth specifications: parental asset information available for years 1985 to 2010 and for 38 percent of the sample
sample.n_observations: 48,071,128 person-years in the widest specification (41,619,160 with positive earnings; 35,077,362 and 31,404,955 respectively with family identifiers; 21,656,217 and 19,660,052 in the parental-wealth samples)
sample.n_individuals: 2,692,479 people born 1946-1977 (2.4 million according to the introduction); 97,932 with depression, 22,694 with BD, 41,813 with schizophrenia

construction_notes: Earnings are the sum of income from wages and self-employment; the text converts earnings from DKK to 2015 dollars using the Danish CPI and the 2015 exchange rate, while the Table 2 note states earnings are measured in nominal DKK
Individuals with positive earnings earn $52,307 on average, with a standard deviation of $83,476 (Table 1)

Diagnosis indicators equal one for people with at least one diagnosis of the condition between 1995 and 2015 and are not mutually exclusive; about 0.4 percent of the population receives diagnoses for more than one type of disorder
The BD indicator is modified in some analyses to include people with either a diagnosis or at least one lithium prescription
# BD episodes counts the number of separate BD diagnoses received between 1995 and 2015 (mean 2.4, median 2)
post equals one for cohorts born after 1956, who turned 20 after lithium was approved in Denmark in 1976

Parental wealth: the percentile of parental assets is computed for each year and the person is assigned their parents' median percentile across all years; parental assets are set to zero for people without asset information
Unemployment: an indicator equal to one if the person was unemployed for one day or more within the year
Event studies normalize the event-time coefficient two years before the diagnosis (d(-2)) to zero
Cohort-specific specifications use two-year birth cohorts between 1946 and 1976 with 1953-54 omitted

claims.statement: Within birth cohort and calendar year, BD is associated with ln(Earnings) in the Danish population aged 20-60 born 1946-1977.

definition.value: Indicator equal to one for individuals who have been diagnosed with bipolar disorder at least once between 1995 and 2015 (ICD-10 codes F31 'Bipolar disorder' and F30 'Manic episode'; the ICD classification does not distinguish BD I from BD II)

timing.value: Time-invariant indicator built from diagnoses recorded between 1 January 1995 and 31 December 2015; the register observation window starts in 1995, after the birth cohorts studied turned 20

definition.value: Natural logarithm of annual earnings, defined as the sum of all wages and income from self-employment; the Table 2 note states earnings are measured in nominal DKK, while the data section states earnings are converted from DKK to 2015 dollars using the Danish CPI and the 2015 exchange rate. Samples for this outcome are restricted to person-years with positive earnings

timing.value: Annual, measured in each person-year at ages 20-60 between 1995 and 2015

magnitude.interpretation: People with BD earn 38 percent less

population.description: Individuals aged 20-60 born in cohorts 1946-1977 in Denmark, observed in person-years between 1995 and 2015, restricted to person-years with positive earnings

definition.value: Indicator equal to one for individuals who have been diagnosed with bipolar disorder at least once between 1995 and 2015 (ICD-10 codes F31 'Bipolar disorder' and F30 'Manic episode'; the ICD classification does not distinguish BD I from BD II)

timing.value: Time-invariant indicator built from diagnoses recorded between 1 January 1995 and 31 December 2015; the register observation window starts in 1995, after the birth cohorts studied turned 20

Samples for this outcome are restricted to person-years with positive earnings

magnitude.interpretation: people with BD who did not have access to treatment earned 42.9 percent less than the population

identification.source_of_variation: Approval of lithium as a maintenance treatment for BD by Denmark's drug authority (Laegemiddelstyrelsen) in 1976: cohorts born after 1956 turned 20 with access to treatment, earlier cohorts did not

key_assumptions.assumption: Parallel trends: differences in outcomes for people with and without BD would have been comparable for cohorts born before and after 1956 in the absence of access to treatment
key_assumptions.supported_by: Cohort-specific estimates show no effects for cohorts born before 1955 (Figures 8-10); Rambachan and Roth (2019) sensitivity analysis in Appendix Figure A6

formal.as_written: Under the identifying assumption that differences in earnings for people with and without BD would have been comparable for cohorts born before and after 1956, the coefficient β on the interaction BDi x postc estimates the effect of access to treatment.

key_assumptions.assumption: Treatment is most important when a person enters their 20s, and lithium was not available at all until 1976 and became available immediately to everyone afterwards
key_assumptions.supported_by: Cohort-specific estimates (Figure 8) show a four-year delay, which the paper reads as gradual diffusion rather than a failure of the design

key_assumptions.assumption: No BD-specific secular confounder: unobservable factors such as reductions in stigmatization or improvements in access to healthcare that change over time do not differentially affect people with BD

identification.source_of_variation: Approval of lithium as a maintenance treatment for BD by Denmark's drug authority (Laegemiddelstyrelsen) in 1976: cohorts born after 1956 turned 20 with access to treatment, earlier cohorts did not

key_assumptions.assumption: Parallel trends: differences in outcomes for people with and without BD would have been comparable for cohorts born before and after 1956 in the absence of access to treatment

formal.as_written: Under the identifying assumption that differences in earnings for people with and without BD would have been comparable for cohorts born before and after 1956, the coefficient β on the interaction BDi x postc estimates the effect of access to treatment.

key_assumptions.assumption: Treatment is most important when a person enters their 20s, and lithium was not available at all until 1976 and became available immediately to everyone afterwards
key_assumptions.supported_by: Cohort-specific estimates (Figure 8) show a four-year delay, which the paper reads as gradual diffusion rather than a failure of the design

key_assumptions.assumption: No BD-specific secular confounder: unobservable factors such as reductions in stigmatization or improvements in access to healthcare that change over time do not differentially affect people with BD

key_assumptions.supported_by: Take-up of lithium documented in Appendix Figure A3

key_assumptions.assumption: Sample conditioning on observed diagnoses: diagnoses are observable only from 1995, so people too ill to survive until their diagnosis is observed are missing and people diagnosed before 1995 only may be assigned to the control group
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper argues this attenuates the estimates; Appendix Figure A5 shows the composition of people with BD is constant across cohorts
